newsitem.title: GERMANY: No breakthroughs, but more talks set on German tax.
newsitem.headline: No breakthroughs, but more talks set on German tax.

text.p: Germany's ruling coalition and Social Democrat (SPD) opposition made no breakthroughs at talks on tax reforms on Tuesday, but did at least agree to meet once again in eight days' time for more negotiations.
"We have the impression that we can reach an agreement, so we should try again," SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said after a three-hour meeting hosted by Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
Kohl said his government would pursue a dual strategy -- to continue the talks while making sure it sticks to its timetable to introduce tax-cutting legislation.
"We are now travelling on two tracks," Kohl said before a meeting of Christian Democrat (CDU/CSU) deputies. "Parallel to legislating we can stop at any time and say: we agree."

Negotiations on Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to cut 30 billion marks ($17.3 billion) in income and corporate taxes are seen as an acid test of Germany's capacity for self-renewal and fitness to lead European monetary union from the front.
Waigel's plans mirror policies pursued by the United States and Britain, while the SPD wants to lay the ground for recovery by stoking consumption.

Waigel said that if the talks on April 23 failed, the two sides would face off again this autumn in parliament's mediation process. The SPD can block most tax measures before then through its control of the upper house of parliament.

A day before next week's talks, Kohl's cabinet will review the second stage of tax cutting legislation which would make big cuts in income and corporate taxes in 1999. A first stage, with smaller tax cuts for 1998, has already entered parliament.

Lafontaine said the meeting -- the third between the two sides since negotiations began in February -- opened the way to possible compromise on five points: cutting the bottom rate of income tax, raising tax allowances and child benefits, cutting corporate tax and trimming so-called labour overheads.
The coalition offered to meet halfway the SPD's demand to cut two percentage points off Germany's jobs insurance charges, but rebuffed opposition charges its tax sums did not add up.
Waigel also offered room for a reduction in the net tax cut by proposing a "30 billion marks minus x" formula which would help limit revenues lost to federal states and municipalities.
"We are interested in any solution which comes as close as possible to 30 billion marks," Waigel said.
Despite progress on some points, there was no clear breakthrough to give government negotiators -- all veterans of German consensus-style politics -- grounds for optimism.
Wolfgang Gerhardt, leader of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said he thought the talks should continue but "a big portion of scepticism remains".
And Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl (CDU), a hardened backroom deal-maker, said: "It is good that we will talk again, but I dare not make a forecast on the outcome."

Sources from the SPD's negotiating team said the outcome of the talks was still completely open. They warned the government against attempting any strong-arm tactics by timing next week's talks after the next cabinet meeting.
"The government misjudges our strength in the legislative process," one SPD source said.
Initial media reaction to the talks, billed by both sides as a last-ditch effort to achieve a compromise, was sceptical.
"My impression was that there were two sides sitting opposite each other who didn't have the nerve to say 'this is pointless'," one commentator for ARD public television said.
